newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-KGB-prisoner in Moscow as Israeli minister.
newsitem.headline: Ex-KGB-prisoner in Moscow as Israeli minister.

text.p: Natan Sharansky returned to Moscow as an honoured Israeli minister on Monday, 10 years after he was freed from a KGB jail and turned over to the West in one of the most dramatic prisoner swaps of the Cold War.

Sharansky, a Soviet-era dissident who served nine years on charges of spying for Washington, was received with honours by Mayor Yuri Luzhkov in the grandeur of Moscow town hall -- a far cry from the squalor of the KGB prison where he spent his last Moscow days.
"As a former Muscovite, forced to leave Moscow, I return as a minister of Israel to a city of free people," he said after signing an agreement of intent to expand trade with Moscow.

Stepping out of the town hall building into the Moscow night, Sharansky ignored waiting limousines and strolled down the city's Tver Street to the house where he was living at the time of his arrest in 1977.
Bundled in a heavy black coat and Russian-style fur hat, he walked up to the old brown door of the apartment block and pulled.
Times have changed. The door was secured against the new hazards of Moscow streets.
Minister for Trade and Industry Sharansky shrugged and went on his way.

His bearing throughout the day as he stood under the chandeliers of state buildings and entered his name in guest books was decidedly that of a politician and diplomat rather than that of a former dissident and prison inmate.
But clearly the visit had a bitter-sweet personal edge.

Sharansky said he would visit old friends who had joined him in human rights demonstrations in the 1970s. On Tuesday he was scheduled to visit the Lefortovo prison where he was held after his arrest. A trip to the labour camp where he served most of his term had, he said, been denied.
"They are embarrassed," he said before the visit. "I asked for the labour camp. They said no...You know, it has changed, but not to the end (completely)."
Sharansky will, however, visit the grave of human rights campaigner Andrei Sakharov, who was sent into internal exile three years after his jailing.

Sharansky, formerly Anatoly Shcharansky, was one of the most prominent political prisoners of the Soviet era. His campaigning for Jewish emigration rights was a bane to the KGB, but the espionage charges raised against him were regarded in the West as severe even by the standards of the time.

After almost 10 years in jail he was released in 1986 at the Glienicke Bridge linking West Berlin with Potsdam in East Germany in one of the last, and certainly the most public, prisoner swaps of the Cold War.

Sharansky crossed the iron bridge to West Berlin on an icy February day in the full glare of dozens of television cameras as a group of Soviet bloc spies crossed in the other direction to East Germany.

Soon afterwards he changed his name to Natan and began a new life in Israel. He says he has never felt any nostalgia for Russia and turned down an invitation to visit soon after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union.
But he says he also harbours no bitterness.

"If I left defeated or humiliated, probably I would feel very vengeful, but the thing is that I always felt...that really it was a great victory and they lost. They were destroyed," he said before the visit.
Sharansky, his features somewhat heavier but largely unchanged from those of the man who crossed the bridge, was accompanied by his elderly mother Ida Milgrom, who had followed her son into exile.
Sharansky was made a minister in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government after the success of his Yisrael ba-Aliya (Israel of Immigration) party in Israel's parliamentary elections last May.

He brought with him a group of 60 Israeli businessmen with the aim of boosting bilateral trade in his five-day visit. His talks with Russian officials will focus on agricultural technology, medical equipment and telecommunications.
Israeli officials say bilateral trade, virtually non-existent five years ago, is now worth about $500 million a year and expanding fast.
